rules.title: Landlord ban on rental application fees
rules.requirement: Massachusetts landlords/lessors may not require rental applicants or incoming tenants to pay application, pet, cleaning, amenity, credit-check, background-check, or other extra upfront fees. Before tenancy, a landlord may ask only for first month’s rent, last month’s rent, a security deposit, and a lock-change fee.
rules.key_value: Only first month’s rent, last month’s rent, security deposit, and lock-change fee may be required before tenancy

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies to lessors before the beginning of a tenancy; the document does not state building-age, unit-count, or occupancy limits.
coverage.summary: Covers Massachusetts lessors/landlords charging prospective or incoming tenants before a tenancy begins.

rules.exemptions: The document says licensed brokers, unlike landlords, can charge application fees under broker rules; landlords may recoup screening costs through rent rather than a direct fee.
rules.penalty: The document reports that in Perry v Equity Residential Management, LLC, a federal district court awarded tenants treble damages and attorney’s fees over unlawful up-front application fees.
rules.interaction: The document contrasts this landlord fee ban with 254 C.M.R. 7, under which licensed brokers may charge fees if they comply with broker regulations.
rules.quoted_span: Massachusetts landlord tenant law spells out the list of charges that landlords may ask tenants to pay at the start of a tenancy: first month’s rent, last month’s rent, security deposit, and lock-change fee. M.G.L. c. 186, §15B. That is all. Landlords are not allowed to request additional charges.

rules.title: Licensed broker fees for prospective tenants
rules.requirement: A licensed broker may charge prospective tenants a fee, including an application-related fee, if the broker complies with broker regulations. The broker must give written notice of the fee amount, when and how it is paid, and whether it depends on a lease being signed, and the applicant must sign or the broker must record refusal.
rules.key_value: Written fee disclosure at first personal meeting

coverage.other_unresolvable: Applies to licensed brokers or salesmen finding dwelling accommodations for prospective tenants for a fee; landlord-brokers may face separate factual/legal issues.
coverage.summary: Covers Massachusetts licensed brokers dealing with prospective residential tenants for a fee.

rules.exemptions: Unlicensed persons may not engage in finding dwelling accommodations for prospective tenants for a fee. The document notes uncertainty for landlords who are also licensed brokers unless operating as a separate bona fide brokerage business.
rules.interaction: The document states brokers may charge fees where landlords generally may not under M.G.L. c. 186, §15B, but cautions that landlord-broker situations lack a definitive Massachusetts appellate ruling.
rules.quoted_span: In addition to holding a valid license, the broker has to tell the applicant in writing the amount of the broker’s fee, the time and manner of payment, and whether it is contingent on the owner and applicant actually entering into a lease or rental agreement.
